title: Effort without strain
hook: the lute string at work: not burned out, not slack (AN 6.55)
tomorrow: how do you put a hard thing kindly in a work message?

segments.voice: Yesterday: honest work, what you hand over and how you hand it. Today, how hard you push while you do it.

One feed praises the five a.m. grind. The next says rest is everything. An old sutta has a monk caught in the same argument. Sona has been pacing his walking meditation so hard that, the story goes, his feet bled, and he's getting nowhere. Alone, he thinks: I'm one of the Buddha's most energetic disciples, and still my mind isn't free. My family has money. Maybe I should go home, enjoy it, and do good with it. The Buddha knows his thought, and comes to see him. Is it ever right to stop pushing so hard? He starts with a question about music.
screen: `THE GRIND, OR REST?` → `SONA'S FEET BLEED.` → `MAYBE I SHOULD GO HOME.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Back when you lived at home, the Buddha asks, were you good at the lute? Yes. When the strings were too tight, was it in tune and easy to play? No. Too slack? No. And when they were neither too tight nor too slack, set at an even pitch? Then it was in tune. In the same way, he says, too much effort leads to restlessness, and too little leads to laziness. So find the even pitch of your effort. Two views live inside the tradition here, and both have texts behind them. The first says: push. Effort is one of the perfections. The Buddha's last words call for diligence. Mahajanaka swam on with no shore in sight. The best case for this side: comfort is persuasive, and stopping can feel like wisdom when it's only tiredness. The second says: ease off. The path is a middle way, and Sona's bleeding feet weren't taking him anywhere. The best case here: strain tightens the mind, and a tight mind can't see. The sutta doesn't crown either one. It hands the choice to a musician's ear: not more, not less, tuned. And the ending is quiet. Sona tunes his effort, and the text says he becomes an arahant.
screen: `TOO TIGHT, TOO SLACK, IN TUNE.` · `VIEW ONE: PUSH. EFFORT IS A PERFECTION.` · `VIEW TWO: EASE OFF. THE MIDDLE WAY.` · `A MUSICIAN'S EAR DECIDES.` · then, large: `TUNE THE STRING.`

segments.voice: Make a tight fist for three breaths and notice what it does to your shoulders and jaw. Let the hand go completely limp. Then close it gently, just enough to hold a pencil, firm and not gripping, and let your whole posture find that same tuning.
Effort without strain: energy set at an even pitch, like a lute string neither too tight nor too slack.
The line to keep: tune the string, not tighter and not looser, until it plays. Three of fifty.

screen: `DAY 1578 COUNTS.` → `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH · 3 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: A HARD THING, KINDLY, IN A WORK MESSAGE?`

howItsDone: Buddhist meditation teachers use the lute simile with students who push too hard or drift, and balancing energy is part of retreat instruction.

match.prompt: tuning the lute — tap the pairs.
pairs: in tune and easy to play
strained so hard he nearly went home

myth: in Buddhism, more effort is always better
too much effort, the Buddha tells Sona, leads to restlessness.
the Buddha used a lute to teach Sona about effort
too tight or too slack, it won't play; set at an even pitch, it's in tune.
the sutta says to ease off whenever practice gets hard
too slack leads to laziness; the point is the pitch, not less effort.

fork.setup: your friend says the lute sutta proves you should never push hard. what's the best case for the other side?
options: effort is a perfection, and a string that's too slack won't play either.
pushing is fine as long as nobody notices you're exhausted.
the sutta is only about music, so it doesn't apply to work.
fork.reveal: the sutta warns both ways: too tight brings restlessness, too slack brings laziness. the push side has texts too: effort is a perfection.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: vina, the stringed instrument in the Buddha's simile to Sona.

trapdoor: what you thought: the middle way means doing everything halfway.
what it means: effort tuned to an even pitch: firm enough to play, loose enough not to snap.
what a scholar hears: in AN 6.55 the Buddha asks Sona Kolivisa about his lute: overaroused energy leads to restlessness, overslack to laziness; Sona then becomes an arahant.
guess: steady energy, neither too tight nor too slack
doing as little as you can get away with
pushing hard until the job is finally done
recall: what you hand over, and how
where you are: the same tools, any job

chat.says: finals + weekend shifts + sketching. ava says i'm doing too much. mom says keep pushing. who's right?
options: Both, kind of. Tune it: drop what's too tight, keep what's steady.
Mom. Effort is a perfection, so push hard until finals are over.
Ava. Strain means it's the wrong path, so drop the extra things.
chat.meaning: The Buddha told Sona effort is like a lute string: too tight brings restlessness, too slack brings laziness. Tune it to an even pitch.

tie.story: The Buddha told Sona, who was straining himself, to tune his effort like a lute: not too tight, not too slack.
tie.friend: Mai can drop one extra shift during finals and keep a steady pace with the rest.
tie.you: is your effort a little tight or a little slack this week?

Sona.meaning: a monk who strained so hard he almost gave up

arahant.meaning: one who has reached full awakening

lute.meaning: a stringed instrument, plucked like a guitar

middle way.meaning: the Buddha's path between harsh strain and easy comfort

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.55, Sona Sutta (Sona's thought of returning to lay life; the simile of the lute; too much energy leads to restlessness, too little to laziness; Sona becomes an arahant)
Vinaya, Mahavagga V.1 (the same story of Sona Kolivisa, whose walking path was stained with blood)

notes: Debate shape: view one (push: effort as a perfection, the last words' call to diligence, Mahajanaka) and view two (ease off: the middle way, Sona's strain) each get their best case; the sutta's answer is tuning, and the lesson ranks neither view.

AN 6.55 paraphrased: Sona's thought ('I am one of the Blessed One's most energetic disciples...', his family's wealth, returning to lay life), the lute questions, and his becoming an arahant. Confirm wording.
The bleeding feet are hedged 'the story goes': the detail appears in the Vinaya (Mahavagga V) telling and commentary rather than the AN 6.55 text itself. Confirm.
